{"title":"Filtering and Querying Records Primer","body":"Begin by reminding the class that a call such as Post.objects.filter(...) produces a QuerySet, not a list, and that this object can be reused and further refined. Emphasise the point made on page 104 that the result of a filtered QuerySet is another QuerySet, which enables chaining of filters as shown in the example with publish__year and author__username. Show a quick live demo chaining two filters and ask the students to predict the SQL that will be generated.

Next, introduce the complementary operations that shape a QuerySet: exclude() to remove unwanted rows and order_by() to control result order. Use the examples from pages 104 and 101 to illustrate a filter followed by an exclude, and a filter followed by order_by('title'), pointing out that the underlying SQL changes accordingly. Explain that these tools are the building blocks for the more complex lookups they will encounter later, such as date parts and related‑field traversals.

Explain that the upcoming unit on building the blog’s archive page will require filtering by year, month, or author, so mastering chaining, exclusion, and ordering now will let the code read naturally. The teacher can pause here and let the class write a one‑line QuerySet that retrieves posts with id 1 or 3, using the __in lookup from page 101.

Check: ask the class, “What does Post.objects.filter(publish__year=2024).exclude(title__startswith='Why') return – all 2024 posts, only those whose titles do not begin with ‘Why’, or nothing at all?” A correct answer confirms they understand that filter narrows then exclude removes matching rows."}
